The non-farm payroll data are based on a survey of employers and the jobless rate is based on a survey of households.

Wall Street economists expected May non-farm payrolls to rise by 219,000 and a jobless rate of 5.0 percent. They also had forecast a 0.4 percent rise in May average hourly earnings and an average workweek of 34.7 hours.
The May unemployment rate, which fell to 4.8 percent, was at its lowest level since October l973 when it hit 4.6 percent. The May jobless rate matched November 1973's 4.8 percent rate.

The May employment report includes the department's annual benchmark revisions to payrolls. The revision is drawn from state unemployment tax records, offering a better picture of the number of people on payrolls than the monthly establishment survey used during the year to estimate payroll growth.
The data also incorporates revised seasonal adjustment factors.

The revised data show that nonfarm payrolls increased by an average of 252,000 a month in the first four months of the year, up from the previously estimated monthly average of 213,5000 for the period.
A Labor Department official said the big upward revision to the April payroll figure -- as well as the March number -- mainly reflects an updating of the department's sampling procedures.
The downward revisions to the payroll data for the first two months of the year, meanwhile, reflect the benchmark revisions and changes in the seasonal adjustment factors.

Katharine Abraham, commissioner of the Bureau of Labor Statistics, said in prepared testimony to Congress that the net effect of the benchmark adjustment was "small" for the data from April 1996 to the present.
Abraham also said that despite the low level of unemployment, the pool of available labor remains sizeable.
"Even with the current high level of labor force participation," she said, "there are more than 66 million people aged 16 or older who are not working or actively seeking work."
She added that the size of the available labor force "is not fixed, but rather depends upon individual decisions based on personal and economic conditions that are constantly changing."

Abraham cited the example of a retired person who may have no interest in finding a job until that person sees a help-wanted sign in a local store and realizes that a conveniently located job is available.
